Australian Residential Property Bearish TA 00:02:33
  • National prices are down 5.2% so far, already comparable to the 2017 (-6.6%) and 2022 corrections, and one of the fastest declines on record — Dave thinks this one will be much bigger because the drivers are different
  • Past corrections were only about rate rises; now there are high rates plus negative gearing changes, CGT changes and property in super becoming much harder, and sentiment has completely flipped
  • Gold Coast has been hit hardest; Hobart has held up — Tasmania is where he would buy now, with Melbourne on his list for when the time is right
  • Adjust for ~4% inflation and the real fall is worse; New Zealand and Canada are the comparable markets (NZ followers say they are down ~45% in real terms)
  • "Fundamentals set the theme, cycles decide the timing" — property tops when fundamentals look unstoppable (low unemployment, strong immigration, shortage); in Canada prices peaked February 2022 and immigration was not cut until about two and a half years later
  • Immigration thesis can change: polls show One Nation leading and the Coalition now also talking cuts
  • Credit sets the price: under 5% of Australian loans are fixed, the average mortgage is now ~$731k at 6.24% (about $45-46k a year in interest versus ~$10k on $550k at 2%)
  • Equity does not protect prices — prices are set at the margin by what the next buyer can borrow (US owners also had large equity in 2006)
  • Land share of property value is at a record ~75% (average ~55%, historical low ~40%); in the US GFC it was land that fell ~70%, not buildings. A return to 60% implies roughly a 10% fall, 50% roughly 20%, 40% roughly 30% — before inflation
  • 18-year cycle: past turns (1972, 1990, 2008) produced 7-15 years of real "dead money"; Phil Anderson's cycle low is October 2028. Property vs Australian shares ratio is in the historically expensive zone (above ~1.16)
  • Practical: shop now if buying a home — distressed sellers may already give the discount you are waiting for (an $8m home bought for ~$4.5m and valued ~$2m higher)

Session Themes

  • Fundamentals set the theme, cycles decide the timing — markets top when fundamentals look best, and fundamentals (like immigration) can change after the top
  • Never get caught at a major cycle top: gold 1980, Microsoft 2000 and health care all show how long the "dead money" lasts, especially in real terms
  • Always adjust for inflation — nominal falls understate the damage
  • Prices are set at the margin by credit, not by owners' equity
  • Divergence is only "blinkers" — wait for price to confirm with a change of market structure
  • Weak breadth is a late-cycle warning, not a timing signal; late cycle can run for months
  • "Do or die" week: the ASX indices, materials, precious metals and crypto are all sitting on key levels at once
  • Trade where the risk/reward is clear — know the entry, the target and exactly where you are wrong
  • Rotation into miners over the metal is the next phase he is positioning for; precious metals seasonality is bullish from October into February-April

Session Themes

  • Yields drive everything right now. A pullback in the US 10-year (to ~4.95-5%) is the catalyst for a final leg up in copper (~$7), gold (~4,400), silver (~$70-73) and US large caps. A later new high in yields then creates the next market low.
  • Late-cycle behaviour: ending diagonals, multiple 1-2s/4-5s, bearish divergence and choppy markets that whipsaw traders. The S&P/Nasdaq can still make new highs while the Dow and Russell have likely topped.
  • Plan for bullish, base and bearish scenarios with probabilities. The best trades are where all three start in the same direction (e.g. gold miners now), then you just execute the plan at critical levels.
  • Divergence time frames: daily divergence means a pullback of several weeks; weekly divergence means several months. Divergence needs a confirmed pivot (3 candles).
  • Know the risk profile of what you own: producers (PDN, Cameco, BHP, S32) can be married and held through risk-off; speculative explorers and ETFs (DYL, URA) should be traded risk-on and exited risk-off.

  • Oil phase framework (supply relief, then re-escalation, with reserve replenishment as a floor). Energy stocks may get one last low.
  • Timeline guess: yields top around Dec-Jan, stocks top 6-8 weeks later, bear market possibly Feb-Mar 2027. Elliott Wave works on structure more than time.

FAQ Fridays

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 09 October 2026
https://academy.masteringthemarkets.com/c/mtm-upcoming-events/faq-fridays-8b6f79 ↗
Bullish Setups: POL, PVT, VBX, DEM
Bearish Setups: MX1, VMC
Neutral / Watching: PAR, BCM, ALV
MX1 (Micro-X) Bearish FA 00:01:02
  • Member asked about the sudden pump. Craig says the business itself hasn't changed: still milestone payments on head CT, lower product sales, Rover hasn't got traction.
  • Perennial (once 10-12% holder) has been selling out over July-August because it's winding up its micro/emerging fund. That's where the selling pressure came from.
  • Red flag: a big holder exiting would normally block trade off-market. Selling on market for months suggests nobody wanted the block.
  • Likes the reset: new CEO Brian (successful in the US) replacing Kingsley, and an external consultant reviewing Rover with every customer. Medical CT and homeland security work are now the focus.
  • The ~$1m contract extension is small and means rescaling the product (more R&D, more delay). Not a reason for a re-rate.
  • ~$8m convertible note funding (announced August) converts around 8c. A cynical read is that the move from ~1.5c makes it much easier to close the note, which they badly need. Director buying around 21-22 Sep.
  • No revenue turnaround, no move to profitability, no commercial conversions and no catalyst on the horizon. Without the run he'd expect it to languish near 4c. "A table without legs" that likely topples, so be very cautious and manage risk tightly.
  • Contrasted with the VBX pattern, where the project improved before each shakeout and run. MX1 has had no fundamental strengthening.
VMC (Venus Metals) Bearish FA 00:16:47
  • Price action followed the announcements: a gap up on the royalty sale, a gap down on the ROX share in-specie distribution, then a run-up into the 17c special dividend (declared 10 Aug).
  • On ex-date it went from a 34c close to a 17-18c open (exactly the dividend) and closed at 16c.
  • Ongoing drift: the company has nothing of substance. It rode the coattails of its ROX shares and the royalty. Henderson Gold and base metals are only at soil-sampling stage, and titanium R&D is going nowhere.
  • Value is now just the remaining ROX shares plus ~$11m cash. No asset to hold the price up, so "a table without legs."
  • Could find a level here or drift to the round 10c number.
  • The only reason to look at it would be an acquisition of a decent project (e.g. $2-5m) that they then drill hard. Consistent with his prior Bearish read (11 Sep).
POL (Polymetals) Bullish FA 00:22:47
  • Member asked whether the FY26 statutory loss is a red flag. Craig: a loss in year one of ramp-up is completely normal, and a loss in year two is still possible.
  • Markers to watch for any miner in ramp-up: progress, then transition to operating cash flow at the mine level. POL has achieved operating cash flow in under a year.
  • Production up 48% QoQ, revenue up ~65% into the June quarter. Shifting from "make it work" to optimising product mix (concentrates plus DSO).
  • Shipment guidance gives a trackable marker: ramping toward a steady state of ~10,000 t/month to port over the next 6-12 months.
  • Big green flag: debt reduced 29% to ~$10m, which rarely happens for new producers in ramp-up.
  • Higher employee and production costs are just context (they're now operating), not a concern. Rates POL as one of the best-quality reporters on the ASX. Builds on his prior Bullish read (6 Oct).
PVT (Pivotal Metals) Bullish FA 00:30:41
  • Horden Lake scoping study came out better than Craig expected on NPV and IRR. CapEx of ~A$411m was in line with expectations (~$380-400m).
  • NPV at base case ~$920m (spot ~$1.3b), post-tax IRR 49%, payback 1.3 years. By-product credits put copper C1 at only ~US$1/lb.
  • Criticism: the base-case copper price of US$5.50/lb is aggressive. He'd prefer stress-testing at ~$4.80-5.00. At ~$4.68, NPV is ~$1b and IRR roughly mid-30s, which is still passable.
  • Polymetallic metallurgy (Cu, Ag, Au, Pd, Ni, Co, Pt) appears solved, and that was always the key question for Horden Lake.
  • The resource is likely much bigger than currently known. EM conductor plates run well below the deepest drilling, and the project was in private hands for ~20 years with little exploration.
  • Next steps: PFS, infill and step-out drilling to push mine life from 10-11 years toward ~15 years. Suggests focusing on Horden over Belleterre exploration.
  • Time-lag risk: probably ~6+ months before the next major study, so plan entries around that. Belleterre exploration could provide interim catalysts.
PAR (Paradigm Biopharmaceuticals) Neutral FA 00:38:34
  • New update on the failed Phase 3: missing data was more frequent at US sites, while observations from Australia, Moldova and Hong Kong appear encouraging. These are preliminary and don't establish efficacy.
  • Independent analysis is now running and could reach different findings from PAR's own.
  • Missing data has to be extrapolated unfavourably, so it could be why the trial failed. It would also be a serious problem for the trial-management CRO.
  • A drug can still fail Phase 3 even after earlier success. That's the point of Phase 3.
  • Don't jump to conclusions either way (that it totally failed, or that it actually works). Wait for the independent review.
  • Note: this is softer than the prior tracker reads (Bearish 25 Sep, Bearish (Unchanged) 29 Sep). Today was a genuinely open "wait and see" rather than a bear call.
VBX (Wedgetail / Weddergoo bauxite) Bullish FA 00:41:20
  • Stock pulled back after the run, the 64c cap raise and the DFS delay to Q1 2027. Craig remains a fan: excellent fundamentals and a very low valuation for a unique ASX bauxite story.
  • The DFS delay is justified: it adds the expanded mining rate and input from shipping, processing, marketing and end-user partners. Better than releasing on time and redoing it 3 months later.
  • An investment framework agreement with a large Chinese group (offtake plus potential project funding) supports a partner-funded build model he likes.
  • Weddergoo bauxite closely mimics Guinean (gold-standard) bauxite but comes with Australian stability. The DFS should look quite different from the PFS (bigger, better deposit). Assume some CapEx inflation.
  • Ryan and family own ~50% and have kept adding. The small free float means fast moves, wide spreads and hard entries, so take a longer-term view and build positions over time.
  • Pattern: strong fundamentals, a no-reason dump (RSI reset), then a run. It's back near a similar level and could fill the small gap below. "Definitely worth being back on our radar." Consistent with his prior Bullish read (25 Sep).
DEM (De.mem) Bullish FA 00:48:57
  • Water treatment, mainly industrial and mining customers in Australia, expanding into residential overseas and possibly in Australia. Industrial is the less competitive, low-hanging fruit.
  • Every acquisition (6-7 in recent years, including Core Chemicals) has improved quickly and been value-accretive.
  • Cash receipts are growing, consistently cash-flow positive, and on track to beat last year. Half-year ~$20m suggests ~$40m for the year (vs ~$25m prior).
  • The challenge is converting EBITDA and revenue growth into solid statutory profitability, which may be what the market is waiting for.
  • Management buying consistently and holding plenty. No red flags.
  • Compared to VYS: undervalued for years before the market re-rated it. "I think it's time." Watch for the profitability transition, gold-sector expansion and residential approvals as catalysts, and use TA to time entry.
BCM (Brazilian Critical Minerals) Neutral FA 00:54:11
  • BFS done and moving into FEED, aiming for a mine in the next couple of years. An earlier MtM find with a big run.
  • Acquiring a magnesium sulfate plant (on care and maintenance since Feb 2026) for ~$1 plus ~A$4m of tax and legacy liabilities payable over ~10 years. This de-risks reagent supply.
  • It doesn't remove sulfuric acid risk, because making magnesium sulfate still needs it (LOT's acid issues show the danger). Supply contracts do come with the plant.
  • Concern: the announcement is light on money detail. The "economic commitment" to restructure and restart is not quantified ($1m or $20m?). It's also unclear why a recently operating plant shut down over financial issues. A study is underway.
  • The project is strong and relatively simple for an ionic clay ISR deposit, positioned as a potential Western-world leader. However, ISR outside China is still in its infancy.
  • Brazilian election and possible government change are a jurisdictional risk to watch. Overall a "good move" with unknown costs. (Prior tracker entry was Frank Watkins' Bearish TA read on 28 Sep, a different educator.)
ALV (Alvo Minerals) Neutral FA 01:00:50
  • Ran ~210% in a day on rare-earth drilling results, after a long pullback from the 2025 run. Craig had expected the focus to stay on VMS copper polymetallic, not rare earths.
  • The recent trading halt "acquisition" turned out to be closing on a project they already had.
  • Good TREO intercepts and strong Dy/Tb grades. Being leaned on as analogous to the Serra Verde takeover (similar geology, slightly bigger area).
  • But it's only a few drill holes against an advanced deposit, so it's "so, so early." Social-media comparisons are "everyone getting really far ahead of themselves."
  • The re-rate is justified from a very depressed base (market cap < ~$10m), but it now needs more drilling and a maiden resource, which takes time.
  • Key question: does management pivot fully to rare earths or keep chasing VMS? Watch the news flow.

Session Themes

  • "Table without legs": price moves with no fundamental improvement underneath (MX1, VMC) tend to fade. Compare with VBX-style dips, where the project kept improving before each run.
  • Always check market cap against what the company actually has. Cash plus shares plus early exploration doesn't support a valuation.
  • Mine ramp-up checklist: losses are normal early. Look for mine-level operating cash flow, trackable shipment and run-rate targets, and debt reduction.
  • Read studies critically: stress-test base-case commodity prices (PVT copper at US$5.50), and press companies that announce deals without quantifying the costs (BCM).
  • Small free-float, high-quality FA names need longer-term position building. Use TA to time entries around transitions (profitability, new markets, studies).
  • Don't extrapolate early drill results into takeover comparisons (ALV vs Serra Verde). Wait for a resource.
  • Biotech: missing trial data is a huge red flag. Wait for independent reviews before drawing conclusions (PAR).
  • Casual MtM meetup at Distillery Road Markets (Gold Coast) on ~24 October with Craig, Jamie and Dave.

Session Themes

  • Skepticism of Elliott Wave — keep it simple: price, volume, OBV
  • The 34-day-high scan's hit rate this week (most names kept running) — sector analysis is unnecessary
  • "The only truth each day is open, high, low, close and volume — everything else is opinion"
  • Process: find the stock → confirm with OBV → fine-tune with market depth → set the stop → size the position by fixed dollar risk → place all orders at once; set the stop at entry, always
  • You need a buy signal (higher highs/lows, 3-month resistance breaks, Darvas boxes, ascending triangles, saucers — not flags or pennants); don't buy because it's "cheap"
  • Patience, individuality, capital gains first (dividends are a bonus); near-zero brokerage encourages overtrading
  • Challenge for next week: bring a stock that's going up

Macro Sunday

Hosted by Tung Nguyen | Sunday 4 October 2026
https://academy.masteringthemarkets.com/c/mtm-upcoming-events/macro-sunday-74756e ↗
Bullish Setups: Emerging Markets, Perth / WA & Darwin Property
Bearish Setups: Australian Economy (GDP per capita / fiscal position), Australian Residential Property (Sydney / Melbourne), Australian Consumer Spending
Neutral / Watching: RBA Cash Rate / AU Interest Rates
Australian Economy (GDP per capita / fiscal position) Bearish Macro 00:05:18
  • GDP per capita is still rising but dislocated below its pre-GFC trend, and successive Treasury projections (2002, 2007, 2015, now) keep slipping — reads it as a secular, not cyclical, decline without structural change (tourism, banking, "dig it up and sell it to China")
  • Payments exceed tax receipts as a % of GDP out to the 2060s; the underlying cash balance is projected negative for the foreseeable future; debt-to-GDP (~40s%) is rising — far from the US (~120%) or the ~100% danger zone, so there's time to fix it
  • 40-50% of tax comes from personal income tax; expects it to fall as wealthy people leave after the capital gains tax and negative gearing changes — the gap then shifts onto those who remain (France as the cautionary end-state: ~€63k employer cost → ~€33k take-home)
  • "The government is spending too much" whenever it runs a deficit, regardless of party
RBA Cash Rate / AU Interest Rates Neutral Macro 00:16:46
  • The 29 Sep hike to 4.6% (highest since Oct 2011) was no surprise — CBA/ANZ moved their forecasts days earlier and the bond market signalled it
  • Fourth rise this year: the average mortgage (~$730k vs ~$350k in 2011) now costs ~$460/month more; the RBA cites the AI boom and the Middle East keeping fuel, fertiliser and food prices high
  • The domino chain: Middle East → oil → inflation → RBA rates — "the 2nd the Middle East opens up again, you'll see interest rates start to fall"
  • Stagflation risk (low growth + high inflation) — last seen in the 1970s; ask which assets did well then — "there's always a bull market somewhere"
Australian Consumer Spending Bearish Macro 00:18:21
  • "The cure for high prices is high prices": even comfortable households are changing behaviour (coffee at home, market shopping, home baking)
  • Real wages are back to 2011 levels — Tung argues Australia is effectively already in a recession on a real purchasing-power basis
  • Food insecurity is rising (13.7% in 2020 → 17.9%), correlated with rate hikes — fewer purchases will eventually pull inflation down
  • Higher rates also raise business borrowing costs and get passed through to renters and non-mortgage holders
Australian Residential Property (Sydney / Melbourne) Bearish Macro 00:33:11
  • Mortgage stress ~32% of mortgage holders, only ~3pts below the GFC high (35.6%, May 2008); the "extremely at risk" cohort is rising but still below the GFC's ~25%
  • Most-stressed postcodes are mostly in Victoria and Sydney (plus one Queensland and one WA suburb)
  • CBA forecasts a ~9% peak-to-trough national fall (Sydney ~13%, Melbourne ~12%) — the worst since 1983; Sydney peaked in February with the first hike; Tung thinks we're about halfway through
  • A secular shift, not a normal cycle: the negative gearing removal (from July next year for established homes) and the CGT discount change turn off investors — friends with 3-7 properties are selling down; over-concentration in property is the biggest single risk he sees
  • More under-30s living at home (22-25s: 35% in 2001 → over half now)
Perth / WA & Darwin Property Bullish Macro 00:36:17
  • Reiterates he's been bullish WA and Darwin/NT for some time as the only areas still growing (one WA suburb nonetheless appears among the mortgage-stress hotspots)
Emerging Markets Bullish Macro 01:05:37
  • Q&A: yes, expects emerging markets to outperform the US over the next 10-20 years (agrees with Jeremy Grantham) — and would almost put Australia in the EM bucket

Session Themes

  • Australia faces a structural/secular growth and fiscal problem; tax changes may drive out high earners and shift the burden to those who remain
  • Rates, inflation and property are downstream of the Middle East/oil — watch Hormuz for the turn
  • The K-shaped economy: boomers (65+) are the only cohort with improving mental health and cognition and falling financial stress; younger cohorts show worse mental health, lower test scores (smartphone dependence), more problematic social-media use, and more living at home
  • A widening university-degree gap (women ahead of men); fewer working-age Australians on benefits and fewer retirees needing the pension
  • Single parents face the most housing stress; couples are more antifragile with dual incomes
  • Brain-drain anecdotes: children of migrants weighing a return to Asia for a better cost of living; offshore structuring (Anthony Overseas' MtM segment)
  • Happiness U-curve bottoms around 50-55 — reaching FIRE earlier brings the upswing forward

Session Themes

  • Use Elliott Wave at the basic level — find the big correction, anchor, count impulses, and pair with divergence; don't over-count corrections
  • Be ready to change probabilities instantly; losses on small-timeframe attempts should be tiny
  • Entry rules: either a reversal (change of structure) or entries off key levels within an established bullish structure — never counter-trend after major breaks
  • Trading for income vs investing: take profits at resistance (NST); scale in/out to manage risk; weekly pivots as hard exits (DYL)
  • Hedging done properly — protection, not speculation; chart the underlying for geared ETFs
  • New traders: use daily change of structure, do 10 logged trades before going lower-timeframe; mark up indices/sectors now and wait for key levels — tread water, protect capital in a tough September

  • Psychology: it's not you — swing/position trading doesn't work in a non-trending, choppy market; adapt rather than quit
  • Chop playbook: buy oversold lows after big pushes down, sell at zigzag zones, lock in profits, trade the daily not the weekly, rotate
  • Be cutthroat with exits; don't get emotionally attached (ARU story); if you wouldn't buy it today, sell it
  • Gold miners vs gold: miners can make higher lows while the metal makes final lows — trade the chart you actually hold
  • Short-term XJO bounce expected for ~2 weeks, then reassess at major resistance

Session Themes

  • Scrip-ratio takeovers: the target trades off the acquirer, there's months of deal risk, and taking cash on market is often best unless you like the acquirer

  • Stay mostly out during uncertain markets; when you do get a buy signal, take it in smaller parcels

  • Sector rotation "takes care of itself" — just buy what's going up; the scan surfaced ~14 sectors; avoid analysis paralysis and "getting married" to stocks
  • Cash is the worst-performing asset long term; overly diversified portfolios get bogged down
  • Psychology: set stops before buying, don't blame tips, stand on your own two feet; the Darvas trader who turned ~$50k into ~$300k then chased options/CFDs and lost it all

Macro Sunday

Hosted by Tung Nguyen | Sunday 27 September 2026
https://academy.masteringthemarkets.com/c/mtm-upcoming-events/macro-sunday-f9bb25 ↗
Bullish Setups: Commodities (broad), Copper, Gold, Silver, Oil (Crude), Fertiliser / Food Commodities, TSLA, Bitcoin / Crypto
Bearish Setups: S&P 500 / Nasdaq, Ride-Share Platforms (Uber / Grab), Legacy Automakers (German / under-invested in EV), US Residential Property
Neutral / Watching: US Treasuries (10Y), Japanese Government Bonds / Japan Capital Repatriation
S&P 500 / Nasdaq Bearish Macro 00:06:01
  • Toppy on every valuation measure he can think of (P/E, price-to-book, price-to-sales), yet tops can keep topping — the Paul Tudor Jones 1999-2000 story
  • Has been out of the market for most of the year with capital elsewhere — "cured of FOMO" after dot-com, the GFC and earlier losses (each FOMO mistake adds a zero)
  • Expects passive buy-and-hold S&P DCA to stop working over the next ~10 years as the demographic tailwind reverses
  • Risk: Japanese and other foreign capital unwinding home if equities take a hit
Commodities (broad) Bullish Macro 00:37:43
  • He and David were bullish before the Iran war because commodities were oversold and unloved for 3-5 years; the war was "the match that lit the tinder"
  • Broad rally across oil, corn, wheat, sugar, gasoline, energy and sulphur
  • Cycle framing: the last commodity bull ran ~2000-2015 (~15 years); this one started ~2020, so it probably runs to at least ~2035
  • "The party's just started" for anyone asking if it's too late
Copper Bullish Macro 00:40:15
  • Supply/demand imbalance charts extend out to 2040 — still early in the cycle
  • Quotes Luke Gromen: "I would rather have copper in my warehouse than cash in my bank"
Gold Bullish Macro 00:57:56
  • ~0.6 of the way through the precious metals bull market; the previous ones lasted 10-11 years (1970-80, 2000-11), so this one (from ~2019) points to ~2030
  • David thinks it could run to ~2032 with a blow-off top (each cycle is bigger/longer); Tung plans to sell a big chunk around 2030 and keep a little in case Dave is right
  • China's US Treasury holdings are at their lowest since 2013 while its 2026 gold imports are the highest in 6+ years — central banks are the deepest pockets
  • Higher real inflation and debasement support the "debasement trade"
Silver Bullish Macro 01:09:21
  • Named with gold and Bitcoin as the assets he "really, really wants to own in this cycle" (debasement trade)
Oil (Crude) Bullish Macro 00:28:19
  • The Hormuz closure is the single biggest macro event — ~20% of global LNG and ~30% of seaborne oil affected, worsened by Houthi disruption
  • A trigger-based event: oil doesn't come down until flows through Hormuz/Red Sea resume
  • Drives inflation, rates "and everything"; US diesel hit harder than gasoline since the war began
Fertiliser / Food Commodities Bullish Macro 00:29:56
  • Through Hormuz: ~44% of sulphur exports, ~31% of urea, ~18% of ammonia — all key fertiliser inputs
  • The conflict has likely meant a missed crop cycle in places → lower yields → higher food prices next season, and famine in some regions
TSLA Bullish Macro 00:21:34
  • Long-term bullish (unsure on short/medium term) on robotaxis (trialling in Austin) and Optimus robots — "reminds me of the iPhone"
  • Robotaxi is a permanent secular shift — owners will rent out their cars when idle
Ride-Share Platforms (Uber / Grab) Bearish Macro 00:22:06
  • Robotaxis upend the taxi/ride-share operating model — in 5-15 years the curve looks like Blockbuster's
Legacy Automakers (German / under-invested in EV) Bearish Macro 00:23:08
  • EVs are a secular shift (~80% of EV owners don't go back to petrol); the EV + hybrid share keeps rising until saturation
  • Carmakers that under-invested in batteries/motors are the "Blockbusters" — German manufacturers are in pain; China is "like the future"
US Treasuries (10Y) Neutral Macro 00:35:39
  • A secular shift in rates: we won't see zero rates "for a very long time" — get used to higher rates as the new normal; the golden era of cheap leverage is ending
  • Fed (Warsh) hiked against Trump's wishes; ~57% chance of another hike next month; end-2026 rate expectations moved from 3.05% to 4.22%
  • The 2-year is leading the Fed higher — expects at least 1, maybe 2 more hikes by December
  • But with the 10-year at its highest since July 2007, bonds now compete with property/stocks for income — expects capital rotation into bonds, especially from cash-rich baby boomers wanting secure income
  • Bond allocation is at a cyclical low (historical pivots near dot-com and the GFC) — bonds may become popular again as a volatility hedge
  • US-China yield divergence (China deflationary, US inflationary) — he suspects the US converges down eventually; foreign buyers stepping back means the US keeps more of its own inflation
Japanese Government Bonds / Japan Capital Repatriation Neutral Macro 00:53:42
  • First time in ~20 years retail Japanese investors are buying JGBs in size — the decades-long borrow-in-yen, invest-offshore arbitrage is reversing
  • If offshore markets dip, Japanese capital could sell the S&P/Nasdaq and head home — a risk for US assets
Bitcoin / Crypto Bullish Macro 00:45:22
  • After the 4-year cycle peaks and crashes (2017, 2021, 2025), money supply is now expanding again — crypto "should do really well next year" on liquidity
  • The ECB's "Pontus" digital euro (interbank tokenised settlement, then a retail digital euro) is really about reducing reliance on US payment rails after the US weaponised its financial system
  • Programmable money can be misused (e.g. Canadian trucker accounts frozen) → physical cash and Bitcoin gain value as hedges against overreach
  • Luke Gromen: Bitcoin may be an early indicator of the debasement tipping point
US Residential Property Bearish Macro 01:06:45
  • The gap between median household income and the income needed to qualify for a loan is bigger than before the GFC — unsustainable
  • Sellers are rising and buyers falling — supply/demand points lower
  • The 10-year Treasury now yields more than most rental properties

Session Themes

  • Macro framework: normal cycles vs secular cycles vs permanent secular shifts; PESTLE drivers; impact sizing → position sizing
  • "Macro-heavy decade": the end of the 40-year falling-rate era, a sovereign debt cycle, deglobalisation, more state intervention (Lyn Alden, Luke Gromen clips)
  • Higher-for-longer rates as a secular shift — leverage-driven strategies get much harder; bonds regain appeal relative to property and stocks
  • Deglobalisation of money: China dumping Treasuries for gold, Japan repatriating, Europe building its own payment rails
  • Hormuz as the dominant trigger-based event — energy, fertiliser, food inflation
  • Psychology: avoid FOMO in toppy markets; only control position sizing and portfolio positioning
  • Tung's preferred assets this cycle: commodities, copper, gold, silver, Bitcoin; long-term secular winners such as TSLA
  • Next week: Australian sentiment research (the "S" in PESTLE)

Session Themes

  • Big-timeframe deep dive: 3M/monthly overbought + bearish crosses on US/Canadian/ASX indices vs reset/bullish commodities, energy, staples, health care and crypto
  • Market breadth in extreme fear while the indices hold up — "this is how the market gets you"
  • Don't panic-sell everything: assess each holding's own phase (excess-phase tops vs early-cycle bottoms), set invalidation levels, tighten stops, keep cash ready
  • Smarter DCA: pause adding to excess-phase assets; increase DCA into big-timeframe buy zones (EEM, staples, health care)
  • ASX risk sits in financials/banks (heavy index weight) — an index correction can drag down sentiment even for strong sectors
  • Rotation from growth to value/hard assets (XSJ/XDJ ratio, Gold/Dow) — like 2000-2013
  • Timeframe matters: the same chart (CBA) is a buy, a range, or an avoid depending on your horizon
  • Crypto: stay long, ride daily structure, ignore short-term blood

Gold Neutral FA 00:09:57
  • Q&A (Mark): why gold and interest rates can rise together — the textbook "rates up, gold down" is only part of the story
  • What matters is real rates: e.g. rates 7% with inflation 8% = -1% real, so purchasing power still erodes, which supports gold
  • Ask *why* rates are rising: commodity shortages, energy prices, fiscal spending, supply chains, currency debasement and geopolitical risk all lift rates and also support gold
  • Over multi-year periods, nominal rates, gold, commodities and equities can all rise together when measured in a depreciating currency
  • Educational framework rather than a trade call (defers to Craig Tapping on the macro detail)

Oil (Crude / sector read from the WA oil & gas conference) Neutral FA 00:01:30
  • Takeaways from the small-cap oil & gas conference: producers "can't believe" current prices, weren't ready for them, and have minimal ability to ramp production into them
  • Industry has little trust prices will last; futures curve agrees — roughly flat for a couple of months, then ramps down to the mid-$70s over 6-9 months once the supply instability resolves
  • Current price is driven by a supply problem, not demand
  • Small caps can still re-rate on project catalysts even if the commodity falls — that's the case for owning them over large caps tethered to price
  • Risk reminder: even the best-possible oil well target has only ~35% odds of success; campaigns are 1-3 wells at $2-3m+ each, much harder than mineral exploration
  • Big Australian players remain risk averse and aren't consolidating small gas plays, unlike overseas (NGY in Indonesia, Jade Gas both have full-field development funded by majors)
BRK Neutral FA 00:08:19

MAT (Matsa Resources) Bearish FA 00:23:54

  • In a trading halt ~3 weeks: contractor claiming unpaid invoices, mine-plan/production/geology problems at Devon (models don't match what's being mined)

Session Themes

  • Small-cap oil & gas vs large caps: catalysts create value independent of commodity price, but exploration odds (~35% at best) and costs are brutal
  • Oil price driven by supply disruption; industry and futures both expect a fade to mid-$70s over 6-9 months
  • Doing the "next level" of FA (debt, capital structure, major-holder leverage) to avoid traps like MAT
  • Reading management behaviour as signals: royalty buybacks and land purchases (SVL) imply confidence in development
  • Ignore HotCopper rumour-mongering around trading halts and cancelled events (PAR)
  • Silver-equivalent grades flatter projects — always check actual silver ounces
  • Stick to your trading rules when a takeover hits your target (GL1)

Uranium (sector read from the WA uranium conference) Neutral FA 00:04:53
  • Industry is "quietly confident" the uranium thematic will play out and is happy to wait — a different mood to the oil industry
  • Same problem as oil & gas: majors aren't backing juniors, no capital push to fast-track developments
  • Craig's long-standing view: most of the ASX uranium sector is inflated/overvalued — "most of these companies have nothing" except ground and an idea
  • Valuation distortions from passive ETF flows (e.g. Cauldron ~$250m market cap on unmineable ground; DYL, and historically BOE/PDN)
  • Industry insiders would like ETFs to discriminate toward developers/producers
  • Signals to watch for capital arriving: majors stepping in like CNNC into Bannerman, PDN acquiring smaller players
DEV (DevEx Resources) Bearish FA 00:07:38
  • Craig saw their first presentation at listing and "they still have nothing" a couple of years on, beyond a larger land holding
  • Market cap (~$155m) is almost the same as AEU, which has two advanced development projects — highlights the sector's valuation disparity
BMN (Bannerman Energy) Bullish FA 00:11:46
  • Presentation "very good"; turned a project he didn't like into one that is now "really actually quite viable" through years of work

DYL (Deep Yellow) Bearish FA 00:12:26
  • "Never been a favourite"; conference showing was lacklustre — scheduled presenter didn't show, CFO filled in
  • Has delayed the final investment decision ~18 months; now says it's waiting for capital markets, labour and inflation to stabilise (not uranium prices) — Craig sees no realistic way those resolve in 2 months
  • Tumas: ~118Mlb at ~255-298 ppm — low grade, needs scale; economics at US$82.5/lb are poor, only robust around US$100-105/lb
  • Financing will be a debt/equity mix — "significantly high chance" of a large cap raise once they hit go
  • ~$1.3bn valuation doesn't make sense to him
AEU (Atomic Eagle) Bullish FA 00:17:57
  • Craig's "find of the conference" — all his questions answered in depth (with Luke); "finally one" undervalued uranium company
  • ~$160-170m market cap for two advanced assets: Zambia (Bannerman-like heap leach) and Nigeria (world-class)
  • Zambia: first feasibility too small (3.5Mtpa, weak NPV at ~US$82); needs ~6Mtpa and a bigger resource — MRE update ~March 2027, new feasibility end 2027
  • Nigeria: ~116Mlb at ~1,282 ppm — same size as DYL's Tumas at 4-5x the grade; ~US$160m and 600,000m of drilling already spent; mining covenant renegotiated and out of international arbitration
  • Nigeria MRE update (modern uranium price) due ~December; redone feasibility Feb-Mar 2027; strategic finance/partner/sale process from ~March 2027 with a hoped outcome Sep-Dec 2027 — US government, CNNC, Russian and European parties already interested
  • Funded to 2028: ~$11m from early option exercise (by 28 Oct) takes cash to ~$23m — no cap raise expected for 12-18 months
  • Chart not reliable due to the late-2025/early-2026 reverse takeover and asset vend-in — prior TA doesn't reflect the new company
  • Explained why a junior would sell a big asset: capital/people/skills required, risk of hostile takeover; proceeds would fund Zambia

Session Themes

  • Uranium conference takeaways: industry quietly confident but capital-starved; ASX uranium valuations are distorted by ETF flows and hype
  • Asset quality vs valuation: DEV/DYL valuations vs AEU's two advanced assets at a similar market cap
  • Low-grade projects need scale and higher commodity prices (DYL, BMN, AEU Zambia)
  • Why juniors sell big assets — capital, people and skills constraints, plus hostile takeover risk
  • After a reverse takeover or major asset vend-in, historic TA no longer reflects the company
  • Leverage + downside protection: cash-backed, resource-backed small caps (CHR)
  • Inflection points (NVU) and regional consolidation (BHM) as sources of re-rating

  • Declined to comment on crypto (won't trade anything off a recognised exchange) and on soft commodities/unfamiliar tickers, deferring those to other MtM educators

US Equity Market (broad exposure) Bearish Macro 01:05:51
  • Shiller CAPE ratio places current valuations more expensive than the 1929 crash peak and only marginally cheaper than the dot-com peak — by objective standards "a very expensive stock market"
  • US margin debt at record levels; Tung's own research found rapid margin-debt expansion preceded the 2000 dot-com crash (80% jump), 2007 GFC (66% jump) and the 2022 bear market (95% jump) — the current expansion read as a similarly serious warning sign
  • Explicitly stated he now has "virtually no exposure" to broad US markets, though he stressed macro is a poor market-timing tool and deferred to David Bird and Craig Tapping for timing signals
  • Concentration risk flagged earlier in the session: roughly 8% of the US stock market is driving all the strength while the other ~92% is flat-to-declining (the "K-shaped" market)
Gold miners Bullish Macro 01:09:10
  • Named as one of the specific exceptions to his otherwise near-zero US market exposure — an area he's deliberately retained alongside copper miners while stepping back from broad US equities
Copper miners Bullish Macro 01:09:10
  • Same treatment as gold miners — kept as targeted exposure despite the broader US equity de-risking, consistent with his "defensive and real assets" positioning
Emerging Markets (Eastern Europe, Latin America) Bullish Macro 00:29:50
  • Personal wealth growth in Eastern Europe described as having "gone gangbusters"; Latin America grouped alongside it as the other standout region
  • Referenced a Jeremy Grantham interview arguing emerging markets should outperform an "overinflated" US market over the next decade
  • Flagged for further research rather than an immediate allocation call — investors still need to separately assess valuations, governance, liquidity, currency exposure and geopolitical risk in each market

Session Themes

  • Australia's "wealth paradox": ranks 3rd globally for median wealth (a better measure of the typical household than the US's average-wealth ranking, which is skewed by billionaires) yet real wages are stagnant and affordability is falling — wealth on the balance sheet doesn't equal cash-flow comfort, since much of it is locked in home equity and superannuation
  • The K-shaped economy: asset owners and higher earners pulling away from everyone else, mirrored in equity markets by a small handful of companies driving index returns while breadth deteriorates; rising credit card balances flagged as a possible stress signal beneath the surface
  • Global wealth concentration: ~1.5% of adults hold over US$1m and control a large share of world wealth, though the proportion of adults with under US$10,000 has fallen over time — a nuance against a purely "rich getting richer" narrative
  • Strategic playbook for the paradox: separate wealth from liquidity (don't assume net worth equals financial independence), build an "antifragile" portfolio stress-tested against falling equities/higher inflation, and use geographical arbitrage carefully (a spectrum from full relocation to partial cost-of-living optimisation, with real tax-residency/visa/healthcare/currency considerations, not just a lifestyle choice)
  • Alternative assets (art, classic cars, collectibles) noted as a surprisingly large allocation among high-net-worth portfolios, valued for their scarcity
  • Psychology: Australians tend to underestimate their global financial standing because they benchmark against local peers rather than global data, amplified by social media's visibility of luxury consumption; the opposite error is assuming high paper wealth alone means emotional readiness for retirement/financial independence
  • Framing device throughout: treat macro conditions like weather — you can't control them, but you can dress for them (position defensively) rather than complain about them

Session Themes

  • Market structure over candle colour: red candles alone never signal a reversal — Dave repeatedly stressed that only a failed recovery, rejection at a key zone, lower high and break of prior structure constitute a genuine change of trend
  • "Zig-zag" framework applied consistently: strong advances are expected to be followed by pullbacks (zags) that reset momentum before the next leg
  • Match timeframe and position sizing to the account's purpose — short-term trading accounts can run more concentrated risk (up to 20% per position, ~1% loss cap) while larger swing/position accounts use smaller allocations (~5% max) to absorb gaps, earnings and announcement risk
  • Rebalancing oversized winners (Woolworths, James Hardie) is about concentration risk and capital efficiency, not a bearish change of view
  • Energy remains the standout long-term theme across the portfolio (Woodside, Santos, Beach), while precious metals/silver equities are viewed as undergoing normal, healthy corrections within an intact bull thesis
  • Psychology: patience through multi-month consolidations and drawdowns was emphasised repeatedly, along with having a pre-defined invalidation plan so decisions are data-driven rather than emotional

Fundamental Analysis Scan with Craig Dickson (Pre-Recorded)

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Tuesday 15 September 2026
Bullish Setups: BKB, MHC, ENP, LPM, PXX, FRS
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: KAO, JAV, FAU, DRR
BKB (Black Bear Minerals) Bullish FA 00:10:19
  • Substantial holder notice: Colin Petroulis (a resource investor with a strong track record — previously built major early stakes in Regis, Vault, Beacon Minerals and Maximus Resources before its takeover) lifted his stake from just over 5% to nearly 10% (bought ~10M more shares in early September).
  • Craig frames Colin as someone who takes large, high-conviction positions before a story is fully proven, then adds again once derisking events (resource updates, scoping studies) land — a pattern that's played out with BKB already (mineral resource update, scoping study on the gold project).
  • Market cap ~$90M with two known projects and a restart study underway.
  • Flagged alongside MHC as the two companies Colin is currently building large stakes in.
MHC (Manhattan Gold Corporation) Bullish FA 00:11:14
  • Same investor (Colin Petroulis) has bought in ~6 times through 2026, lifting his stake from ~5% to 11.111%.
  • ~$20M market cap; >200,000oz foreign (NI-style)-compliant gold resource in Canada, in a well-serviced region near major operators (Anglo and others).
  • Recent RC drilling results: 15m @ 5g/t Au (within a larger mineralised interval), 74m @ 1.6g/t, 51m @ 1.8g/t — broad, shallow mineralisation supportive of open-pit potential.
  • New drilling has also found gold outside and below the existing resource boundary — geological interpretation shows multiple plunging lenses with room to grow.
  • Catalyst: conversion of the existing NI-style foreign estimate to a JORC-compliant resource, likely to include the new drilling and increase contained ounces.
  • In a trading halt for a "material" capital raise (expected ~$5M) at time of recording, due back on market the next day.
KAO Neutral FA 00:18:04
  • Share price raced from around $2.20 (cap raise price) up past $2.50, taking market cap to roughly $100M, on the back of visible copper mineralisation (chalcocite and malachite) in two early holes.
  • Important caveat: there are no assay results yet — the run is based purely on visual observation of sulfides, which Craig says is historically an unreliable basis to chase.
  • Chalcocite typically hosts very high copper grades and malachite is also a strong visual indicator, which explains the market's excitement, but metallurgical test work to separate/recover the copper from this mineralisation style can be challenging.
  • Company capitalised on the run with a $20M raise at $2.20/share, so is now well funded to drill aggressively.
  • Craig's explicit stance: don't chase this — watch from the sidelines if you weren't in early; early-stage speculative re-ratings like this have a high chance of giving back gains just as fast ("a table without legs").
FLG Informational FA 00:23:47
  • Trading halt today was purely administrative: the half-year report was lodged two minutes late (due to a delay at the outsourced accounting/admin provider), triggering an automatic one-day suspension.
  • Confirmed directly by FLG's Paul (MD) to Craig — no underlying issue with the business.
  • Stock resumes trading the next day with no concerns.
ENP (Entropy) Bullish FA 00:25:03
  • 12-week data released for the first cohort (6 patients) of its IV psilocin trial for treatment-resistant binge eating disorder (patients with the condition for up to 15 years, unresponsive to prior treatments).
  • Clinically meaningful improvement sustained across the full 12 weeks for all patients — not just an acute effect.
  • 50% of patients had zero binge-eating episodes over the entire 84-day follow-up.
  • Binge-eating episodes down 74% at 4 weeks and 73% at 12 weeks vs baseline; anxiety down 50%, depression down 42%, quality of life up 61%.
  • Cohort 2 will trial a shorter dosing session (~60 minutes vs ~120–140 minutes) to test whether similar efficacy can be achieved — a meaningful commercial lever (more patients/day, lower cost per treatment) if it holds up; results expected toward year-end.
  • Company also has a broader "basket study" underway and a new agreement with a prominent US researcher to run trials there, seen as a step toward an FDA pathway.
  • Craig's view: thesis keeps strengthening and the stock remains under-followed relative to the news flow.
JAV Neutral FA 00:30:20
  • Trading halt announced "pending an announcement in connection with a potential change in control transaction."
  • Background: JAV holds a right-to-mine agreement with Mega Resources (Mega pays $25M to get into production, recoups it from profits, then profits split 50/50 — or 70/30 in JAV's favour if a new resource is converted into a mining project).
  • David Garrity (who runs Forrestania Resources, FRS) had already taken a ~7% personal stake in JAV, an early signal something was changing.
  • Craig's working theory: this is connected to the broader Forrestania-linked consolidation web (see FRS/FAU below) rather than a straight takeover by Mega, though he flags Mega could alternatively just acquire JAV outright to avoid giving up the 70/30 profit split.
  • Outcome expected to be clarified around Wednesday (17 September) — genuinely uncertain at time of recording.
FRS (Forrestania Resources) Bullish FA 00:31:21
  • Described as building a gold-producing company "at breakneck speed" — achieving in ~2 years what typically takes other companies 8–10 years — including restarting two processing mills.
  • Same day as the JAV/FAU trading halts, FRS announced a strategic agreement with Mega Resources: rights to purchase and process up to 2M tonnes of ore over 2 years, plus a 5-year master services agreement letting FRS contract Mega quickly across its wider mining network.
  • Craig sees FRS using management-linked companies (JAV, FAU) to further its consolidation agenda, expecting these to eventually be wrapped into FRS.
  • Takeover of ZMC is proving harder than anticipated, keeping FRS occupied there — part of why Craig doesn't think FRS is the one taking direct control of JAV right now.
  • Note: FRS's history with TG6 was hostile, so any future move there may face shareholder pushback.
FAU (1st AU / 1st Gold) Neutral FA 00:33:40
  • Also entered a trading halt today for a "potential change of control transaction" — identical wording to JAV, announced the same day.
  • Management overlaps with Forrestania; FAU already has an ore purchase agreement with Forrestania to supply the Lake Johnson or Edna May processing facilities.
  • Holds a modest ~100,000oz gold deposit and has been consolidating surrounding ground.
  • Craig sees FAU and JAV as connected pieces of the same Forrestania-linked story (possibly a scrip merger given FAU isn't much bigger than JAV by market cap), but stresses this is speculative and he could be wrong.
LPM (Lithium Plus Minerals) Bullish FA 00:40:23
  • ~$19–20M market cap; Craig is looking for leveraged, under-the-radar lithium exposure with real project quality (not just theme-chasing).
  • Pursuing a DSO (direct shipping ore) model rather than building a concentrator — avoids a ~$250–400M capex build (compare to DVP's Pioneer Dome, which needed ~$30–40M just for its own DSO option) and only needs an estimated ~$80–100M to develop as an underground operation.
  • Located ~80km from port/processing, directly next to Core Lithium's (CXO) operations at BP33 — much shorter haul than DVP's Esperance route.
  • Grade of 1.5% — above the ~1.2% Craig cites as the typical "comfortable" threshold for WA hard-rock lithium.
  • Granted Mining Lease; scoping study due end of September (management told Craig it's essentially ready, just being finalised).
  • Strong relationships flagged as a differentiator: "Cattle" (a major established lithium industry player) is a holding in the company, and management (including Jason, who also runs PXX) has strong China/international lithium industry links — funding for the build is said to be largely covered already via partners/major shareholder.
  • Side context: Core Lithium (CXO) previously shut down and is reworking its flowsheet; Craig speculates CXO could eventually be a consolidator (or acquisition target) for nearby DSO-style ground including LPM's Lay project.
PXX Bullish FA 00:52:16
  • Recent high-grade copper results triggered questions — grades described as "scary good," high enough that some labs can't accurately assay at that level without specialised equipment.
  • Caveat: the standout holes are twin holes (drilled next to previously assayed holes), so not new discovery info — but the new assays (done with equipment capable of handling higher grades) suggest historical assays across the deposit may have been under-reading grade, meaning a planned re-assay campaign could lift the project's overall grade profile.
  • Separately, new (non-twin) holes confirmed mineralisation extending 500m below surface with a 170m depth extension — genuine growth to the deposit (Caribou Dome).
  • Northern Star is funding the entire Caribou Dome/Alaska Range program; if funded through to completion, Northern Star ends up owning ~80% of Alaska Range, at no cost to PXX.
  • ~10,000m of drilling still to come; Craig wants to see consistency across the rest of the program before getting more definitive, but calls it "still such a great project."
DRR (Deterra Royalties) Neutral FA 00:57:25
  • ~$2B market cap, PE ~13 (fair value range) — one of only two ASX-listed royalty/streaming names Craig is aware of (the other being tiny-cap DGR).
  • FY26 NPAT $164M, up slightly on last year; pays consistent dividends twice yearly.
  • Surprised the market by selling all three of its precious metal royalty/streaming assets (for combined proceeds+income of ~$90M, versus an acquisition cost of ~$73–75M — a net gain of ~$15–20M over a couple of years).
  • Remaining assets: Mining Area C iron ore royalty (current core income) and a royalty over Thacker Pass (massive US lithium project, still in construction, targeted for completion late 2027 then 1–2 years of ramp-up) — DRR earns nothing from Thacker Pass until it's producing.
  • Has ~$350M of debt capacity plus some cash and needs to redeploy it — potential avenues include a new streaming/royalty deal or a direct stake (has a small position in Anson Resources' Paradox Basin lithium project via a 2% net smelter royalty, also not near-term).
  • Craig's framing: worth watching as the established ASX royalty/streaming play, but currently a "one-trick pony" on income until they deploy capital into something new.

Session Themes

  • A live example of Forrestania Resources' consolidation strategy playing out in real time — management-linked companies (JAV, FAU) hitting simultaneous change-of-control trading halts alongside a new Forrestania–Mega Resources ore-purchase and services agreement, fitting a pattern Craig has been tracking in his articles for weeks.
  • Gold sector M&A/toll-milling structures (right-to-mine agreements, ore purchase deals) continuing to proliferate as mills restart across WA, against a backdrop of gold futures remaining in contango out to 2032.
  • Lithium DSO (direct shipping ore) as a lower-capex way to get exposure to the lithium theme, using DVP/Pioneer Dome as the template and LPM as this session's example of a small, well-connected, undervalued leverage play.
  • Repeated caution around chasing momentum on unconfirmed/visual-only results (KAO) versus backing projects with real assay data, known resources or funded drill programs (MHC, PXX).
  • "Follow the money" investor tracking — using substantial holder notices (Colin Petroulis in BKB/MHC) as a signal-generation tool, based on the investor's historical track record.
  • Educational detour on CDIs (CHESS Depositary Interests) and dual-listed/flow-through share structures, answering a leftover FAQ Friday question.
  • Royalty/streaming companies (DRR) explained as a distinct business model investors should evaluate like any other business — income streams, costs, growth opportunities and debt.

Session Themes

  • Trading psychology after a volatile week: don't let one bad week shake confidence — reflect on what went wrong (over-confidence, over-exposure, not taking partial profits) rather than dwelling on losses.
  • "Playing defense" doesn't mean going to cash outright — it means closing recently-opened/weak positions, tightening stops on extended winners, and taking partial profits, which naturally raises cash (currently ~15% cash) as stops get hit.
  • Portfolio diversification: keep no single theme/asset class above roughly 20–25% of the portfolio; aim for 4–5 independent "sure bets" rather than one concentrated theme, since not every thesis will play out (crypto's halving-cycle "sure thing" cited as a cautionary example).
  • Seasonality: historically ~80% of major market tops (1929 Depression, 1987 crash, 2000 dot-com, 2008 GFC) occurred in the September–January window, with the second half of September specifically flagged as the higher-risk period this year.
  • Reviews his long-term portfolio only four times a year (quarter-ends) since historically most major trend changes cluster around quarter-end/earnings/index-rebalance periods — everything in between is "noise."
  • Broad market read: after a strong 5–6 week rally into August, US and Australian equities (and most ASX sectors) are showing bearish divergences and, in several cases, confirmed changes in market structure, while precious metals, AUD and bond yields diverge higher — consistent with his view that 2026 is a "defense" year and a possible rotation into hard assets.
  • Reiterated framework used across almost every chart: pullbacks into a prior support/resistance zone ("zag zone") are healthy and expected; a failure to hold that zone, or sellers not becoming buyers there, is what confirms a genuine change in market structure.
  • Announced a major end-of-quarter "deep dive" review session in ~2 weeks' time (no Q&A planned given its scope).

PAR Bullish FA 00:24:21

NOX Neutral FA 00:45:28
  • Oliver asked about Knox (NOX) after CSL reported positive results using a related drug/target, alongside NOX's own drug validation signs.
  • Craig's key framework: biotech must be assessed by stage — the CSL-referenced work is still lab/pre-clinical (petri dish/early animal model), not yet in human trials; only the "Soft SKN" asset has reached Phase 1/clinical stage.
  • Soft SKN: completed Phase 1, now planning an open-label extension study (starts Q1 2027) ahead of Phase 2 planning (targeted mid-2028) — an unusually long gap Craig says he doesn't fully understand and would want explained by the company directly.

VMC Bearish FA 00:53:33

  • Post-dividend, VMC is left with a market cap of only ~$25-30m and effectively no active project — "these guys have nothing" beyond one very early-stage asset.

SBM Bullish FA 00:55:15
  • Lisa asked about SBM's deal to divest its non-Canadian operations.
  • Craig likes the move — exits a difficult jurisdiction and nets ~$400m to fund the Canadian growth pipeline; company is considering (not yet committed to) a 13c/share dividend and a ~100m-share buyback — Craig warns reneging on either promise would hit the share price hard.
  • Deal completion timeline is lengthy — expected close between January and March 2027 pending approvals/votes.
  • Canada plan has two legs: (1) restarting a mill to process existing gold stockpiles for near-term cash (modest scale, restart targeted by year-end), and (2) the "15 Mile" project — PFS due September, DFS to follow, final investment decision targeted mid-2027; management's relative silence on financing suggests confidence in funding much of it from existing cash plus a likely equity raise rather than heavy debt.
  • Ongoing royalty income (~$11m, then 16/26/28 outlook) will partially offset the cash-flow gap left by the divested asset, but won't fully cover it alone.
  • Craig's overall take: "a good move… resets the business… gives them a better focus, a consistent focus… a better jurisdiction to work in."

Session Themes

  • Reading ASX company filings: how to interpret substantial holder notices, cleansing notices, and change-of-holder filings — mostly noise in large caps (institutional cycling/short-covering) but genuinely useful signal in small caps for tracking real support or exits.
  • Order book literacy: buy/sell walls and headline "more buyers than sellers" counts can be manipulated (stacking orders far from the touch, hidden/off-book orders); useful mainly for gauging queue position and confirming support/resistance already visible on the chart, not as a standalone signal — especially unreliable around opening/closing auctions.
  • Share buybacks are a double-edged sword: they don't necessarily put a floor under price (companies are incentivised to let price drift lower to buy more shares per dollar) and can flatter per-share metrics (EPS) purely by shrinking share count rather than genuine profit growth.
  • Biotech and early-growth-tech investing both hinge on understanding company "stages" — pre-clinical vs. clinical, and how far a business really is from commercialisation/profitability — recurring framework applied to both TTT and NOX this session.
  • Hot Copper forums: useful for finding genuinely knowledgeable posters (geologists, industry insiders) but require heavy skepticism — most posts reflect emotional attachment or misunderstanding of market cap/valuation mechanics rather than real analysis.

Session Themes

  • Central behavioural theme: overcome "analysis paralysis" — form your own view, act on a defined setup, and use stops to manage uncertainty rather than waiting for every analyst/educator to agree. Differing Elliott Wave counts are useful as contingency context, not a reason to freeze.

  • Recommended exercise: complete ten independently selected trades using very low capital, then stop and review — study winners for common strengths and losers for repeated errors, even from a small sample.
  • Financials (CBA, NAB, ANZ) were the session's clearest "stand aside" sector — multiple names broke key pivots/triangles during the call itself, reinforcing the "don't be in financials until they show life" message.
  • Energy and coal (Woodside, Worley, Yancoal, Whitehaven) stood out as the strongest sector, with the practical challenge being a lack of laggards — the answer was to wait for pullbacks on leaders rather than chase.
  • Recurring risk process: define entry, technical reasoning, size, stop and time horizon up front; exit without negotiation once invalidated, then reassess the chart rather than defend the original thesis.

Session Themes

  • Central theme: next week's Fed and Bank of Japan decisions (plus ECB/BoE developments) are the dominant catalyst for almost every market discussed — Craig repeatedly frames setups around "if they hike" vs. "if they hold" scenarios, with a dedicated macro session planned to cover all four combinations.
  • Elliott Wave best practice reinforced repeatedly: always maintain both a bullish and a bearish count with explicit invalidation levels (e.g. gold's $4283/$4697), so a trade can be taken and managed regardless of which count plays out, as long as both scenarios agree on the near-term path.
  • Broad "risk on vs. risk off" framing applied across uranium, emerging markets, crypto and equities — speculative/developer-stage names (URA, uranium explorers, EM small caps) carry much more two-way risk than producers/mega-caps (Paladin, large-cap defensives) in the current environment.
  • Sector rotation / economic cycle framework shared and explained in detail: markets are judged to have moved from "recovery" (small/micro caps thriving, second half of 2025) back into "contraction" after the war restarted rate-hike risk in February — in contraction, mega caps and defensive sectors (healthcare, staples, utilities) tend to outperform, not speculative small caps.
  • Commodity-price versus commodity-producer divergence was a recurring theme: agricultural and uranium commodity prices are viewed bullishly, but the operating companies (GrainCorp, Elders, non-producer uranium developers) are flagged as lagging due to high input costs or speculative premium/discount dynamics.
  • Gold miners (GDX) vs. gold itself, and copper vs. gold ratio, were both used as "leadership" indicators — watching for a change in which asset is leading to infer the next phase of the broader commodity cycle.
  • Reminder on chart reliability: heavily diluted small caps (RML) should be assessed on fundamentals rather than technicals, since repeated capital raises distort historical price structure.

Session Themes

  • Same chart, different valid biases: a short-term trader, a swing trader and a long-term investor can each be "right" about the same stock (CBA example) because their timeframes and goals differ.
  • Follow your own plan, not someone else's opinion or analysis — illustrated with Nickel Industries (ignoring bearish outside calls while the stop holds) and CSL (Jamie's disciplined earnings exit still framed as "good trading" even after the stock popped 18%).
  • Normal zig-zag-zig market structure: drawdowns and pullbacks ("zags") are expected and shouldn't trigger an exit on their own — only an actual change of market structure should.
  • Turning positions "risk-free" by moving stops to breakeven once structure confirms (Boss Energy, NextDC, Beach Energy) is a recurring risk-management technique.
  • Portfolio rotation and opportunity cost: rotating out of an extended winner (PLS, up ~500%) into a comparatively less extended one (BHP) is framed as a risk/reward decision, not something to regret even when the sold position later runs further.
  • Position sizing discipline: trimming James Hardie back to standard ~2.5% sizing after a big run and recycling the capital into a better risk/reward setup (WiseTech).
  • Good trading is about process, not outcome — a trade that follows the plan and loses is framed as better than a lucky win without a plan.
  • Community reminder: keep chart requests to 1–2 tickers via the Q&A section so requests can be worked through fairly; take advantage of the community for peer feedback.
  • Melbourne Live event flagged as near sold out (200-person cap), with new content being unveiled there for the first time.

Session Themes

  • Central lesson: always test whether an announcement's headline is actually backed up by the supporting data — don't take headlines (e.g. "discovery," "high grade") at face value.
  • Key vocabulary for spotting early-stage/target-generation announcements: "surface sampling," "rock chips," "historical," "potential," "drill ready," absence of intercept lengths.
  • Grade smearing / the "nugget effect" — how a single narrow, extremely high-grade interval can distort a broader average grade (West Coast Silver case study).
  • Distinguishing genuine production milestones from full ramp-up (Core Lithium's first concentrate vs. sustained production).
  • Funding and cap-raise risk as a recurring theme across explorers (Raptor, Krakatoa) — a likely raise can be a reason to wait for a better entry.
  • "Context is everything" — a good announcement doesn't always move the price (if already priced in or dilution is expected), and a middling one sometimes does.
  • Teaser for the evening's FAQ Fridays-style call: a deep dive on capital raisings and share purchase plans (SPPs).

Fundamental Analysis Scan with Craig Dickson

SHV (Select Harvests) Bullish FA 00:32:55

VR8 Neutral FA 00:36:39

  • Strategy pivot: abandoning the high-value downstream product/DSO routes in favour of pyrometallurgy (producing pig iron + high-grade vanadium slag) — a simpler, more conventional pathway.

E25 (Element 25) Bullish FA 00:43:35

  • Long-term case: potential downstream manganese processing facility/relationship in the US on top of the near-term production offtake.
  • Typical share-price pattern flagged: run-up into first production, then a pullback through the ramp-up phase as risk increases (cap raise risk being part of that).
BRE (Brazilian Rare Earths) Neutral FA 00:48:09
  • Market cap just over $1B — one of the larger-scale, higher-quality rare earth names (unlike the smaller-cap rare earth plays discussed recently).
  • New scoping study (out in August) showed strong headline numbers: post-tax NPV ~US$6B, 1.1 year payback, ~90% IRR.
  • CapEx is large — ~US$969M (~A$1.5-1.6B) for the full downstream route, or a cheaper ~US$91M "fast-track" option to get to concentrate production sooner.
  • Grade compares favourably to Mountain Pass, Lynas and Arafura.
  • Complexity is high — plan includes downstream separation (hydrometallurgy) plus potential by-product credits from uranium, scandium, niobium and tantalum (uranium pricing/revenue not yet modelled in the scoping study).
  • Pilot plant is commissioned and running its first ore now — Craig calls the next 6-12 months of metallurgical test work the "make or break" period for the project.
  • Company's stated production timeline (~3 years) looks very optimistic to Craig — he'd assume 5+ years is more realistic.

Session Themes

  • Deep-dive explainer on capital raising mechanics: clean placements vs multi-tranche raises vs SPPs/rights issues, why tranche 2 and SPP settlement periods create share-price overhang, and typical 4-6 week (placement) vs 1 month+ (SPP) settlement timelines.
  • "Context is everything" when reading announcements — a headline guidance miss can still represent a very strong underlying result (SHV example).
  • ASX/investor conditioning toward US/China biotech and meditech deals, with Craig noting Europe is structurally underrated for aging, wealthier populations.
  • Recurring theme across several near-term producers (AKA, E25, VR8) of funding/ramp-up risk and the likelihood of further cap raises even after a major financing is secured.
  • Trade-off in rare earth and vanadium projects between simple, low-capex product routes and higher-value but much more complex downstream/chemistry-heavy processing.
  • Value of following management interviews (Alkane's Nick) for insight into how larger resource companies actually assess project quality (free cash flow, AIC over AISC).
